Where it began

Graeme Smith was born on 1 February 1981 in Johannesburg to Scottish parents, and went to King Edward VII School. He represented South Africa at Under-19 level in three Tests and seven one-day games, and the South African Cricket Annual named him one of its Cricketers of the Year for the 2001–02 season.

His first Test was against Australia at Cape Town in 2002, and he made 68 at number three in the second innings. In only his third Test he was moved up to open against Bangladesh, and he marked the promotion with 200.

The player

After the 2003 World Cup he was made captain at 22, with just eight Tests behind him. Nobody younger had led South Africa. That summer in England he made 277 at Edgbaston and 259 at Lord's in successive Tests. The Lord's innings beat a record for a visiting batsman there that Don Bradman had set in 1930. He finished the series with 714 runs and shared the player of the series award with Andrew Flintoff.

He played 117 Tests from 2002 to 2014 and scored 9,265 runs at 48.26, with 27 hundreds. He captained in 109 Tests and won 53 of them, and he was the first captain to reach 50 Test wins. Two series stand out. In 2008 his unbeaten 154 at Edgbaston sealed South Africa's first series win in England since 1965. Later that year his side became the first from South Africa to win a Test series in Australia, starting with a chase of 414 at Perth in which he made 108.

What made him special

A tall left-hander, he led from the front. With Herschelle Gibbs he formed South Africa's most prolific opening pair, and he played in all four of his country's 300-run opening stands. The biggest, 415 with Neil McKenzie at Chittagong in 2008, beat a first-wicket record that had stood since 1956. He was a superb catcher too, with 169 catches in his 117 Tests.

His bowling was another story. Eight Test wickets at 110.62 suggest he was right to leave that side of things to others.

Away from the middle

He captained Somerset for part of 2005, made a triple hundred for them (311 against Leicestershire) and led them to the Twenty20 Cup. In 2008 he opened for Rajasthan Royals in the first IPL under Shane Warne, and from 2013 he captained Surrey. He was named a Wisden Cricketer of the Year, and in 2019 MCC made him an honorary life member.

After his playing days he moved into commentary and was appointed commissioner of the SA20 league. He is a devoted Liverpool supporter.

And finally

His 100th Test as captain, against Pakistan, fell on his 32nd birthday, and he had already made a hundred in his 100th Test. Not every great innings ended in style, though. At Trent Bridge in 2003 he went back to a ball from Andrew Flintoff and trod on his own stumps. Even the best openers sometimes take one step too many.
